title: Gamification and student motivation

papers.title: Gamified quizzes and intrinsic motivation among Malaysian undergraduates
papers.introduction: Asks whether gamified quizzes raise undergraduates' intrinsic motivation.
papers.methodology: Cross-sectional survey of 320 undergraduates at two public universities; PLS-SEM.
papers.results: Gamified quiz use predicted intrinsic motivation (beta = 0.38, p < .001).
papers.discussion: Read as support for SDT; authors urge autonomy-supportive quiz design.

papers.title: Leaderboards in secondary science classrooms
papers.introduction: Tests how leaderboards affect engagement in secondary science lessons.
papers.methodology: Quasi-experiment with 140 pupils in Penang over 8 weeks.
papers.results: Not retrieved (results section missing from the available copy).
papers.discussion: Warns that leaderboards may demotivate low-performing pupils.

papers.title: Students' lived experience of gamified learning
papers.introduction: Explores how students experience gamified courses (PhD thesis, Universiti Example).
papers.results: Three themes emerged: competition, autonomy and fatigue.
papers.discussion: Gamification fatigue appears after about week 6 of a course.

papers.title: Badges and engagement in MOOCs: a review
papers.introduction: Reviews the evidence on digital badges in MOOCs.
papers.results: 24 of 40 studies linked badges to short-term gains in completion.
papers.discussion: Long-term effects of badges remain unclear.

synthesis: Motivation theories anchor three of the four papers, each a different one: Self-Determination Theory (Tan & Rahman, 2023), Flow theory (Ali & Wong, 2024) and Goal-setting theory (Ali, 2021); Lee (2022) states no framework. Methods are mixed: two quantitative studies (a survey with PLS-SEM and a quasi-experiment), one qualitative thesis and one narrative review, with no mixed-methods or longitudinal design. Quartile balance could not be judged: none of the three journals was found in Scimago, so all are Unranked/Unavailable, and the fourth item is a thesis; check the journal names against Scopus before relying on these sources. Recurring tension: game elements show short-term motivational gains (beta = 0.38 for quizzes; completion gains in 24 of 40 badge studies) while two papers flag downsides (leaderboards demotivating low performers; fatigue after about week 6). Gaps your study could fill: effects beyond a single semester, which element (quizzes, leaderboards, badges) drives motivation, how prior achievement moderates leaderboard effects, and a mixed-methods design linking survey effects to student experience. The Lee (2022) results must be retrieved before its effect can be compared.
